title: Exercise 3: Labour Market Flows
text:
This exercise presents different methods for examining labour market flows - ie the transitions between one kind of involvement in paid work (for example, full-time employed) to another one (for example, economically inactive) using longitudinal data from the Labour Force Survey - in this case the 2 Quarter LFS.
Some of the estimates used in this exercise relate to figures published by ONS on the ‘Labour market flows NSA’ sheet in Table X02. NSA stands for ‘non seasonally adjusted’, as we will be examining flows that took place between two quarters (as opposed to seasonally adjusted yearly averages).
Learning outcomes:

Becoming familiar with Two Quarter Longitudinal Labour Force Survey data
Being able to use longitudinal weights
Being able to compute proportions with their confidence intervals
Being able to estimate labour market flows using different methods



This exercise relies on the Two-Quarter LFS Longitudinal Dataset for July - December 2024, which is available from the UK Data Service (Study number 9348).



First we load the packages required for the exercise:

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

We suggest that you create a folder named LFS_exercises as the working directory for this exercise – where syntax files and other materials will be stored. After downloading the data, save it in an easily accessible location within LFS_exercises, such as a subfolder named Data. Then open the LLFS dataset:

setwd ("~") # Set the working directory

### Importing the Stata format dataset 
lfs2q_js24 <- read_dta(
        "Data/lfs/UKDA-9348-stata/stata/stata13/lgwt24_2q_js24_od24_eul.dta"
                    ) 
#  Create a smaller, easier to handle,  dataset
# Convert categorical variables into factors for easier handling

dataex3 <- lfs2q_js24|> 
             select(LGWT24, AGE2, AGES2, EMPLEN1,EMPLEN2, FLOW, 
                    SEX, ILODEFR1, ILODEFR2,INCAC051, INCAC052 
                    ) |> 
               mutate( 
                    across(
                           c(AGES2:INCAC052),
                           \(x) as_factor(x)
                           )
                      )

What is the FLOW variable?
Why do some variables have a suffix of 1 or 2?




FLOW measures labour market flows, that is the transitions between economic activity statuses
The suffix in most variables indicates the wave ie the quarter at which it was recorded.







In order to match the definition used by the ONS for their published estimates, we will use the exi]sting FLOW variable but only consider respondents aged 16-64. We will then weight the data with the longitudinal weight LGWT24. This time we will be looking at transitions between employment broadly defined and self-employment from wave 1 to wave 2.

title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
In this exercise, we will recreate an ONS labour market estimate published online in the table EMP07 Temporary Employees. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey (QLFS).
Learning outcomes:

To become more familiar with quarterly LFS datasets.
To become familiar with weighted population counts and their confidence interval

Do the frequencies change noticeably when the weight is applied?
Using the code we used to create JobTmp above as guide, create a variable to indicate those working part time and examine their weighted and unweighted frequencies. You are going to need this variable later.

The LFS weights also account for the survey’s sample design: individuals who had a lower chance of being selected are given higher weights to correct for that. They also help adjust for different levels of non-response across subgroups in the population, which means the results are more likely to reflect the population accurately.

title: Exercise 3: Labour Market Flows

This time we will be looking at transitions between employment broadly defined and self-employment from wave 1 to wave 2.
